reason: The quotation survives; the NOTE does not, and must be rewritten before the card ships. I downloaded the Gutenberg text the verifier named (pg35698.txt, 826 KB, Letters of John Keats to His Family and Friends, ed. Sidney Colvin, 1891) and read letter CXIII in place. Its heading is "CXIII.--TO FANNY KEATS." and it is dated "Winchester, August 28 [1819]", so the locator is exactly right. Colvin's sentence runs: "Give me Books, fruit, French wine and fine weather and a little music out of doors, played by somebody I do not know--not pay the price of one's time for a jig--but a little chance music: and I can pass a summer very quietly without caring much about Fat Louis, fat Regent or the Duke of Wellington." The card's wording is that text character for character up to "know", including the capital B on Books against lowercase fruit, and the closing full stop replaces Colvin's dash, which the note does declare. The verifier was also right to reject the circulating form, which the Calendar For Life bank carries at cflId 340 as "Give me books, French wine, fruit, fine weather and a little music played out of doors by somebody I do not know": that version reorders the list, drops the capital, and moves "out of doors" onto the wrong side of the verb. Gates: shipped.js returns shipped [] and near [], Keats at 1 for the year (month 4), cap 3, not banned; in scope, Correspondence, 1891 edition of an 1819 letter, publishable; source line 130 characters, leads with the name, no dash, no straight double quote. The defect is this. The note asserts "Colvin's edition reads Books, fruit, French wine, and then a little music out of doors, played by somebody I do not know. That wording is restored here." That is not what Colvin reads and not what the card prints: both contain "and fine weather" between the wine and the music. A note that misquotes the edition it is defending is the same failure the standard exists to prevent, only in miniature, and it will read as a confident false citation to anyone who checks. Replace it with something like: "Colvin's text reads Give me Books, fruit, French wine and fine weather and a little music out of doors, played by somebody I do not know, and the sentence runs on, so the closing full stop is the card's. The circulating version reorders the list and moves out of doors, and is not Keats." One editorial remark, not a fault: of the four cards this is the weakest fit for a month on Truth and Clarity, being a list of pleasures rather than plain seeing, though it is at least plain speech.
